name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
title: Digital Signals of Mental Health
answer: Digital signals of mental health means using data people already generate through phones, wearables, keyboards, voice, and online activity to estimate mood, sleep, stress, cognition, or risk. In telemedicine and triage, these signals can support intake, symptom tracking, and decisions about who needs a human clinician sooner. The topic overlaps with passive sensing, digital phenotyping, affective computing, and remote monitoring. This atlas tracks 1000 medical AI models, and the mental health signal models are a clinically sensitive part of that wider inventory. It is not a diagnosis by itself and not a replacement for clinical interview.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Digital signals of mental health means using data people already generate through phones, wearables, keyboards, voice, and online activity to estimate mood, sleep, stress, cognition, or risk. In telemedicine and triage, these signals can support intake, symptom tracking, and decisions about who needs a human clinician sooner. The topic overlaps with passive sensing, digital phenotyping, affective computing, and remote monitoring. This atlas tracks 1000 medical AI models, and the mental health signal models are a clinically sensitive part of that wider inventory. It is not a diagnosis by itself and not a replacement for clinical interview.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Smartphones and wearables are the main collection layer, with accelerometers, GPS, screen time, call and text metadata, heart rate, sleep, and voice samples. Data moves through mobile apps, secure APIs, cloud storage, and sometimes on-device inference to reduce raw data exposure. Telemedicine platforms and electronic health records may receive summaries or alerts rather than continuous raw streams. Infrastructure choices affect battery life, bandwidth, privacy, and whether a signal is available when a patient is offline. Some systems rely on consumer devices, others on clinical-grade sensors, and the difference matters for validation.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams start with a clinical question, such as detecting worsening depression or triaging crisis risk, then choose signals that are feasible and meaningful. They extract features from raw sensor and interaction logs, or train sequence models on the raw streams, and compare against validated questionnaires or clinician assessments. Because labels are scarce and noisy, studies often use self-report scales, ecological momentary assessment, or chart review, with careful attention to missing data and confounding. Models are evaluated for sensitivity, specificity, calibration, and fairness across age, gender, language, and diagnosis groups. Deployment usually keeps a human in the loop for any escalation.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Digital mental health signals touch sensitive data, so consent, purpose limitation, data minimization, and withdrawal rights are central. Provenance matters because a model trained on one app's users may not transfer to another clinic, device, or population. Risks include false alarms, missed crises, stigma, re-identification, and commercial use of intimate behavioral data. The atlas tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows why documentation, audit trails, and clear lines of responsibility are part of the work. Regulation varies by jurisdiction, and the atlas's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect that patchwork.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The near-term direction is more integration with telemedicine triage, where a signal prompts a check-in or routes a patient to a crisis service, typically with human review. Research is moving toward multimodal models that combine voice, sleep, activity, and text, and toward personal baselines rather than single universal thresholds. On-device processing and federated learning may reduce raw data sharing, though validation and equity gaps remain. Regulators and clinicians will likely demand prospective trials, drift monitoring, and plain-language explanations for patients. The field's credibility depends on showing that these signals improve care without increasing surveillance or harm.
